entry: Nigerian musician and political activist. He is regarded as the principal innovator of Afrobeat, a genre combining West African music with American [[Funk|funk]] and [[Jazz|jazz]]. In the 1970s his band Africa '70 became popular in Nigeria, and Kuti was an outspoken critic of the country's military juntas. In 1970 he founded the Kalakuta Republic commune, which declared itself independent from military rule. A 1977 army raid destroyed the commune and killed his mother, Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti, a [[Women's rights|women's rights]] activist. Kuti was jailed by the government of Muhammadu Buhari in 1984 and released after 20 months. He continued to record and perform through the 1980s and 1990s, and since his death his music has been reissued under the supervision of his son, Femi Kuti. He was posthumously inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] after two previous nominations.

Group of rock-forming aluminium tectosilicate minerals. Feldspars make up about 60% of the [[Earth's crust|Earth's crust]] and 41% of the Earth's continental crust by weight. They also contain other cations such as sodium, calcium, potassium or barium. The most common members are the plagioclase (sodium-calcium) feldspars and the alkali (potassium-sodium) feldspars. Feldspars crystallize from [[Magma|magma]] as intrusive and extrusive [[Igneous rock|igneous rocks]] and are also present in many [[Metamorphic rock|metamorphic]] and [[Sedimentary rock|sedimentary rocks]]. Rock formed almost entirely of calcic plagioclase is known as anorthosite. The ratio of alkali feldspar to plagioclase feldspar, together with the proportion of [[Quartz|quartz]], is the basis for the QAPF classification of igneous rock.

Family of [[Mammal|mammals]] in the order [[Carnivora]], the cats. The 41 officially recognized extant species show the greatest diversity in fur patterns of all terrestrial carnivores. Cats have retractile claws, slender muscular bodies, strong flexible forelimbs and a powerful bite, and all are obligate carnivores. Most are solitary predators that ambush or stalk their prey. The living family is divided into two subfamilies. The Pantherinae include five *Panthera* and two *Neofelis* species, while the Felinae include the other 34 species in 12 genera. The first cats emerged during the Oligocene, about 25 million years ago. The domestic cat (*Felis catus*) is the only fully domesticated member of the family.

Austrian skydiver and BASE jumper. He was known for jumping from a helium balloon in the [[Stratosphere|stratosphere]] and landing in New Mexico on October 14, 2012, as part of the [[Red Bull]] Stratos project. The jump set world records, including one for an estimated 39 km (24 mi) skydive, and he became the first person to break the sound barrier relative to the surface without vehicular power on his descent. On July 20, 2003, he became the first person to skydive across the [[English Channel]] with a carbon fiber wing. He died in a paragliding accident in Italy.

German composer, pianist, organist and conductor of the early Romantic era. His best-known works include the overture and incidental music for *A Midsummer Night's Dream*, including the "Wedding March," the oratorio *Elijah*, and the melody used in the Christmas carol "Hark! The Herald Angels Sing." His performance of the *St. Matthew Passion* in 1829 revived interest in the music of [[Johann Sebastian Bach]]. Although his grandfather was the Jewish philosopher Moses Mendelssohn, he was baptized into the Reformed Christian church at age seven. His essentially conservative tastes set him apart from [[Franz Liszt]] and [[Richard Wagner]], and the [[Leipzig]] Conservatory he founded became a bastion of this outlook. After a long decline in his reputation, partly due to [[Antisemitism|antisemitism]] in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, his creative originality has been re-evaluated.

Oral sex act involving stimulation of the penis with the mouth. It may be performed as [[Foreplay|foreplay]] before intercourse or as an intimate sexual act in its own right. Fellatio creates a risk of [[Sexually transmitted infection|sexually transmitted infections]], although the risk is significantly lower than that of vaginal or anal sex, especially for [[HIV]] transmission. Most countries do not ban the practice, though some cultures may consider it [[Taboo|taboo]]. Commonly, people do not view oral sex as affecting the [[Virginity|virginity]] of either partner, though opinions vary.

Sex of an organism that produces ova (♀), the egg cells that fuse with sperm during sexual reproduction. A female's gametes are larger than a male's. In the oogamous pattern found in humans, the female gamete is much larger than the male and cannot move. In species with two sexes, sex may be determined by [[Chromosome|sex chromosomes]] or by environmental conditions, and most female mammals, including human females, have two X chromosomes. In some species females can reproduce without males, for example through [[Parthenogenesis]]. In humans the word can also refer to gender in the social sense.

Expulsion of fluid from the Skene's gland during or before [[Orgasm|orgasm]]. It is also called squirting, although the two are distinct: squirting is a sudden expulsion of liquid that partly comes from the [[Bladder|bladder]] and contains urine. Research has been limited by highly selected participants, small samples and the lack of common definitions. In questionnaire surveys, 35–50% of women report having experienced the gushing of fluid during orgasm. There is substantial evidence that the Skene's gland is the source, although the exact nature of the fluid remains controversial. Its function is unclear.

Cutting or removal of some or all of the [[Vulva|vulva]] for non-medical reasons. As of 2024, [[UNICEF]] estimated that more than 230 million girls and women worldwide had been subjected to one or more types of the practice, including over 144 million in Africa and over 80 million in Asia. Progress is too slow and is outpaced by population growth. The practice is typically performed by a traditional cutter with a blade, often without [[Anesthesia|anesthesia]]. In infibulation, the vulva is closed and a small hole is left for urine and menstrual fluid. The practice is rooted in gender inequality, attempts to control female sexuality, and ideas about purity and beauty. It has no known health benefits and can cause recurrent infections, chronic pain and complications in childbirth. It has been outlawed or restricted in most countries where it occurs, although the laws are often poorly enforced.

Internal and external sex organs of the human female. The internal tract consists of the [[Vagina|vagina]], [[Uterus|uterus]] and fallopian tubes, and it is prone to infections. During the [[Menstruation|menstrual]] cycle an [[Ovary|ovary]] releases an ovum that travels through a fallopian tube toward the uterus. Fertilization usually occurs in a fallopian tube, and the resulting blastocyst implants in the uterine wall to begin gestation. If no fertilization occurs, the uterine lining is shed in menstruation. The external organs, known as the vulva, include the labia and the [[Clitoris|clitoris]]. The cervix connects the uterus to the vagina and dilates during childbirth. Later in life, [[Menopause|menopause]] halts menstruation as the ovaries stop releasing eggs.

Personal care products for menstruation, vaginal discharge and other functions of the [[Vulva|vulva]] and [[Vagina|vagina]]. Disposable products include menstrual pads, pantyliners and tampons. Reusable products include menstrual cups, cloth pads, period underwear and menstrual sponges. Products meant to cleanse the vulva or vagina include douches, feminine wipes and [[Soap|soap]]. Many health professionals advise against douching, which can change the balance of vaginal flora and acidity. The vagina defends itself largely through resident [[Bacteria|bacteria]], which keep the pH acidic, outcompete pathogens and generate antimicrobial compounds such as bacteriocin. Cleansing products may also cause allergic reactions and irritation.

Freestanding structure that encloses an area, usually built from posts joined by boards, wire, rails or netting. A fence differs from a [[Wall|wall]] in not having a solid foundation along its whole length. A ditch, sometimes filled with water to form a [[Moat|moat]], is an alternative. Fences serve many purposes: agricultural fencing keeps [[Livestock|livestock]] in and predators out, sound barriers reduce noise pollution, and privacy fencing provides security. Common constructions include chain-link fencing, made of wires woven together; picket fences, generally waist-high and decorative; and split-rail fences. Fences are believed to date to about 3500 BCE in Mesopotamia, where they protected livestock.

Combat sport of sword fighting in three disciplines: foil, épée and sabre. Each discipline has its own blade and rules, and points are scored by making contact with the opponent with one's sword. Modern fencing developed from historical European swordsmanship; the Italian school altered classical fencing, and the French school later refined that system. Competitive fencing has been featured in every modern [[Olympic Games|Olympics]]. The sport is governed by the Fédération Internationale d'Escrime (FIE), headquartered in Lausanne, Switzerland, which has 155 national federations. In pool rounds, bouts are fenced to five hits or a single period of three minutes. Knockout bouts continue until one fencer scores 15 hits or the nine-minute fencing time expires.

Smallest fox species (*Vulpes zerda*), native to the [[Desert|deserts]] of North Africa. Its unusually large ears dissipate heat and help it listen for underground prey. The fennec mainly eats [[Insect|insects]], small mammals and birds. Families dig sand burrows as large as 120 sq m (1,300 sq ft). Population figures are not precisely known, but sightings suggest the species is not threatened with [[Extinction|extinction]]. It is commonly trapped for exhibition or sale in North Africa and is considered an exotic pet in some parts of the world.

Flowering perennial herb (*Foeniculum vulgare*) in the [[Apiaceae|carrot family]]. It is native to the shores of the Mediterranean and has become widely naturalized elsewhere, especially on dry soils near the sea coast and on riverbanks. The stem can grow to 2.1 meters (7 feet) tall and bears yellow flowers and feathery leaves. Its licorice-like flavor comes from anethole, also found in [[Anise|anise]], and fennel and anise are primary ingredients of [[Absinthe|absinthe]]. Fennel is widely cultivated for its edible leaves and fruits. Florence fennel, a [[Cultivar|cultivar]] with a swollen, bulb-like stem base, is eaten as a vegetable.

Highly potent synthetic [[Opioid|opioid]] used primarily as a pain medication. It is 50 to 100 times more potent than [[Morphine|morphine]]. Its main clinical use is pain management for cancer patients and people recovering from [[Surgery|surgery]]. It is often mixed with [[Heroin|heroin]] or [[Cocaine|cocaine]], or disguised as pharmaceutical pills, which complicates the treatment of overdoses. Synthetic opioid overdose deaths, primarily involving fentanyl, increased from 2,600 in 2011 to 70,601 in 2021 in the United States.

Annual plant in the family [[Fabaceae]] (*Trigonella foenum-graecum*). It most likely originated in the Near East and is cultivated worldwide as a semiarid crop. Its leaves and seeds have been used in cooking since ancient times and are common in dishes from the [[Indian subcontinent|Indian subcontinent]]. Seeds have been recovered from the tomb of [[Tutankhamun]]. Although it is a common [[Dietary supplement|dietary supplement]], no significant clinical evidence suggests therapeutic properties, and it can cause serious adverse effects, including allergic reactions.

French general and Marshal of France. He was Supreme Allied Commander on the [[Western Front (World War I)|Western Front]] from March 1918, coordinating French, British and American efforts. Foch commanded the French Ninth Army at the Marne in 1914, which raised his prestige. He halted a renewed German advance on Paris at the Second Battle of the Marne, and he stopped the German spring offensive of 1918 and launched a war-winning counterattack. On November 11, 1918, he accepted the German request for an armistice. Foch considered the [[Treaty of Versailles]] too lenient on Germany. [[Winston Churchill]] attributed to him the apocryphal remark, "This is not Peace. It is an Armistice for twenty years."

King of Aragon (1479–1516) and co-ruler of Castile with his wife, [[Isabella I of Castile|Isabella I]]. Ferdinand is considered the de facto first king of Spain, although Castile and Aragon remained separate kingdoms until the Nueva Planta decrees of 1707–1716. Their marriage in 1469 is regarded as the cornerstone of the Spanish monarchy, and the couple are known as the Catholic Monarchs. Together they sponsored the first voyage of [[Christopher Columbus]] in 1492, the year they defeated [[Granada]], the last Muslim state in Western Europe, completing the [[Reconquista]]. In March 1492 they issued the Alhambra Decree, which ordered Jews to convert or leave Castile and Aragon. In 1507 he became regent of Castile for his daughter Joanna, and in 1512 he conquered most of the Kingdom of Navarre.

Holy Roman Emperor from 1556 to 1564. Born and raised in Spain, he ruled the Austrian hereditary lands of the [[House of Habsburg|Habsburgs]] for his elder brother, Emperor Charles V. He was archduke of Austria from 1521 and king of [[Bohemia]] from 1526. The key events of his reign were the [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] advance into Central Europe, which began in the 1520s, and the Protestant [[Reformation|Reformation]], which led to several wars of religion. Although not a military leader, Ferdinand was a capable organizer who built a centralized government for Austria, Hungary and Bohemia instead of pursuing a universal monarchy. His approach to religious matters was flexible, moderate and tolerant. His motto was *Fiat iustitia, et pereat mundus* ("Let justice be done, though the world perish").

Portuguese explorer who led the 1519–1522 Spanish expedition to the East Indies. Magellan was the first European to encounter the [[Strait of Magellan|strait]] that bears his name, and the expedition made the first European crossing of the [[Pacific Ocean]]. It also made the first known European contact with the [[Philippines]], where Magellan was killed in battle. Under the command of the Spanish navigator Juan Sebastián Elcano, the expedition reached the Spice Islands, and the *Victoria* returned to Spain in 1522, completing the first circumnavigation of the Earth. Magellan had served the Portuguese Crown in Asia, but King Manuel I of Portugal declined to support his plan to reach the Moluccas by sailing west, and Magellan offered it to Charles I of Spain.

Filipino lawyer and politician, president of the [[Philippines]] from 1965 to 1986. From 1972 to 1981 he ruled under martial law, embracing a policy he called "constitutional authoritarianism." Debt, inflation and Philippine involvement in the [[Vietnam War]] brought unrest during his second term, and the regime used violence against political opposition, including Muslims and suspected communists. Official results in the 1986 snap election declared Marcos the victor, but allegations of mass electoral fraud led to the People Power Revolution, and on the advice of [[Ronald Reagan]] the family fled to [[Hawaii]]. His tenure is widely described as a kleptocracy marked by corruption, extravagance and brutality, and he remains a controversial figure. His children, including Bongbong Marcos, who has been president since 2022, have denied accusations of [[Human rights|human rights]] violations by their parents.

Swiss linguist, semiotician and philosopher. He is widely considered one of the founders of 20th-century [[Linguistics|linguistics]] and, with [[Charles Sanders Peirce]], one of the two major founders of [[Semiotics|semiotics]], which he called semiology. He published little during his lifetime. Students compiled his lectures posthumously as *Course in General Linguistics* (1916), which described language as a system of signs defined by differences within its structure rather than by individual uses. Its emphasis on synchronic over diachronic analysis shifted the field from historical philology toward the study of structure. Leonard Bloomfield wrote that Saussure had given "the theoretical basis for a science of human speech." His ideas have influenced [[Anthropology|anthropology]], philosophy, [[Psychology|psychology]] and sociology.

Persian poet, author of the epic *Shahnameh* (Book of Kings). The *Shahnameh* is one of the world's longest epic poems created by a single poet and the greatest epic of the Persian-speaking countries. It narrates the legendary and historical kings of Iran from primordial times to the Arab Muslim conquest in the 7th century. Ferdowsi completed it in 995, three years before [[Mahmud of Ghazni|Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni]] acceded to the throne, and completed a second edition in 1010. The poem draws on ancient Iranian religious traditions, including [[Zoroastrianism]], and links pre-Islamic Iranian culture with post-Islamic culture. Ferdowsi is celebrated as one of the most influential figures of [[Persian literature]].
